Tell your students to ONLY approach to help if they are completely sure that the electricity has been turned off.
Walk through the response: call 9-1-1, provide CPR if necessary, and treat any visible burns with clean dry dressings.
IMPORTANT: all electrical burn patients need medical follow up because internal damage may not be visible on the surface.

tips.title: ENVIRONMENTAL EMERGENCIES
tips.body:
Environmental emergencies can range from minor incidents to life-threatening situations.
In this section, you will introduce students to bites from animals, insects, and humans, along with other environmental hazards that can cause harm. Explain that proper first aid helps reduce infection risk, control pain, and prevent complications.
Let students know that each of these emergencies will be covered in the following slides so they understand how to recognize them and respond appropriately.

tips.title: Animal or Human Bite
tips.body:
Cover the two primary concerns with any bite:
• Managing bleeding
• Preventing infection.
Walk students through the response steps:
• Wash the wound gently with soap and water
• Control bleeding with pressure
• Call a healthcare provider for any wound that breaks the skin.
Inform your students that in childcare, human bites between toddlers are common. Clean the area, monitor for infection, and notify the parents of both children.

tips.title: Snake Bite
tips.body:
Share the four venomous species native to the US on the slide, then focus on busting these common myths:
Myth: Should I suck out the venom?
Reality: Do NOT suck out venom!
Myth: Should I apply ice to the snake bite?
Reality: Do NOT apply ice!
Myth: Should I apply a tourniquet to keep the venom from spreading?
Reality: Do NOT use a tight tourniquet!
Go through the correct response: keep the child calm and still, wash the wound, remove rings and tight clothing from the bitten limb, apply a loose light bandage to immobilize the area, and wait for EMS.

tips.title: Bee Sting
tips.body:
Teach the correct removal technique: use the edge of a credit card and scrape in the opposite direction of entry. Emphasize that pinching the stinger can squeeze more venom into the skin and should be avoided.
After removal, the response is to wash the area, apply ice, and monitor for signs of an allergic reaction. Remind students to refer back to the anaphylaxis and EpiPen training from earlier in the course if a severe reaction develops.

tips.title: Spider or Scorpion Bite
tips.body:
Let students know that most spider and scorpion bites cause only mild reactions, but highlight the exceptions: black widow and brown recluse bites can make someone very ill.
The general response is to wash the area, apply ice, and monitor. If the child develops severe pain, muscle cramps, or difficulty breathing, call 911.

tips.title: Tick Bite
tips.body:
Walk students through the correct removal technique using fine-tipped tweezers as described on the slide. Stress that they should not twist or jerk the tick, as this can leave parts embedded in the skin.
Cover the warning signs to watch for in the weeks following a bite: a bull's-eye rash or flu-like symptoms, both of which may indicate a tick-borne illness.

tips.title: Marine Bites and Stings
tips.body:
Use the slide to walk students through the response steps for a jellyfish sting. Address any questions or myths students may have regarding treatment.
Close with the IMPORTANT callout: Call 911 immediately if a bite or sting from any marine animal causes severe pain, trouble breathing, signs of shock, or a severe allergic reaction and notify the parent or guardian.

tips.title: Drowning
tips.body:
Open with the stat: drowning is the number one cause of death for children ages 1 to 4.
This is especially important for childcare workers in the room. Explain what real drowning looks like, it rarely matches what they have seen in movies. Describe the signs: head low in the water, mouth at water level, body vertical, gasping, and arms flailing. Emphasize that they should never enter the water if it puts them at risk; reaching or throwing a flotation device is the safer approach.
Cover the CPR difference for drowning: start with 2 rescue breaths before beginning the standard 30:2 cycle. Explain that drowning is primarily an oxygen problem, which is why rescue breaths come first.

tips.title: Poisoning
tips.body:
Children swallowing medications, cleaning products, or other household items they are not supposed to have is one of the most common reasons Poison Control is contacted.
Cover the two response paths:
• If alert and stable: Call Poison Control
• If not alert: Call 9-1-1
-
Encourage caregivers to save the number in for Poison Control in their phone: 1-800-222-1222
Stress the rule: DO NOT INDUCE VOMITING.

tips.title: Opioids and Overdose
tips.body:
Teach students to look for common signs of a possible opioid overdose, such as drug paraphernalia nearby, slow or stopped breathing, pinpoint pupils, blue or gray skin, and unresponsiveness. Explain that the first step is to call 9-1-1 and get an AED right away.
Introduce Narcan as the brand name for naloxone, a medicine that reverses the effects of opioids by blocking them in the body and helping restore normal breathing.
Keep it simple and reassure students that Narcan (naloxone) is safe, has no serious effect on someone who is not having an opioid overdose, and should be given when an overdose is suspected. Show students how to give Narcan nasal spray as described on the slide.

tips.title: TEMPERATURE RELATED ILLNESS
tips.body:
Temperature-related illnesses happen when the body gets too hot or too cold and can no longer regulate its temperature properly. The severity of these conditions progresses in stages over time. Early recognition is key.
Children are more susceptible to temperature extremes than adults. Introduce students to the most common heat and cold emergencies and explain that the next slides will cover the signs, risks, and first aid steps for each.

tips.title: Heat Related Illness
tips.body:
Teach heat-related illness as a progression where each stage can escalate to the next if warning signs are ignored. Walk through signs and treatment for all four stages using the slide:
• Dehydration
• Heat Cramps
• Heat Exhaustion
• Heat Stroke

tips.title: Cold Related Illness
tips.body:
Start with frostbite. Explain that frostbite is the local freezing of skin and the tissue underneath it. It most commonly affects fingers, toes, the nose, and ears. Point out key signs.
Then cover hypothermia; it occurs when the body's core temperature drops below 95°F (35°C). It happens when the body loses heat faster than it can produce it, causing the core temperature to drop and organs to slow down.

tips.title: Conclusion
tips.body:
Remind students that being prepared is the key to emergency response. Prevention, awareness, early action, and staying calm can make all the difference. Encourage them to share what they learned with coworkers and families.
Thank them for being here and for taking this training seriously. Completing this course already puts them ahead, and they should be proud of the commitment they are making to protect and care for children.

tips.title: Introduction
tips.body:
• Introduce yourself and any additional instructors. Give a brief reason why you teach CPR.
• Ask students to introduce themselves and share their names and their role (childcare provider, teacher, babysitter, etc). A quick round of names helps you learn who is in the room.
• Cover housekeeping: restroom location, class length, breaks, practice area, skills evaluation, and AED location in the building.
Tell students: “Today we’ll focus on CPR and AED use for infants and children. This course is for lay rescuers who care for children and need to act quickly before EMS arrives.”

tips.title: WHY ARE WE HERE?
tips.body:
This is your opening slide, and it sets the tone for the entire class. Your goal here is to answer a simple question for your students: Why are we here? You want to establish the purpose of the course right away and get them engaged.
Start by getting their reason for being there.
• Ask your class: "Why are you here today?" and let a few students answer.
Whether it is for childcare, teaching, a new baby, camp work, or job requirements, acknowledge every reason. Then connect the training to their role by saying something like:
• “Most of you care for children in some way. You might work in a daycare, school, camp, home, or family setting. If a child becomes unresponsive and stops breathing normally, you might be the first person there. This course teaches you what to do in those first few minutes."
• This small step makes the class feel personal to them rather than like a generic requirement.
It is also important to acknowledge the sobering reality that many individuals who receive CPR do not survive. This is often due to delays in administering CPR after their heart stops. All cases involving CPR can be hard to handle emotionally and this is especially true when it involves an infant or a child.
Pediatric Age Guidelines for CPR
• INFANT – Under 1 year old
• CHILD – 1 year old until signs of puberty

tips.title: Heart Attack vs Cardiac Arrest
tips.body:
Engage the room right away by asking: "Who can tell me the difference between a heart attack and cardiac arrest?"
• Pause for a few seconds and let a few answers come out. If a student's answer is close, affirm it and build on it. If nobody raises their hand, that is perfectly fine. Just say something like, "That is exactly why we are here, let's break it down."
• A lot of people mix up a heart attack and cardiac arrest, and your students need to be able to separate them quickly because the first actions for each are different.
Now teach the difference in plain language: A heart attack happens when blood flow to part of the heart gets blocked. Think of it like a plumbing problem. The heart usually keeps pumping, and the child is often still awake and breathing. Do not spend too long here. Inform the students they will hear more about heart attack warning signs in the First Aid section.
Close with: "For this CPR section, remember one thing: if the child or infant is down and not breathing normally, that is your signal to act."

tips.title: What is CPR
tips.body:
Your goal here is to clear up the medical jargon. New students often feel intimidated by the science, so your job is to translate it into a simple, mechanical concept. Use a confident, encouraging tone to set the stage for the hands-on practice coming later.
Break down the words: Cardiopulmonary Resuscitation
• Cardio for the heart
• Pulmonary for the lungs
• Resuscitation, which we just call 'reviving' or bringing someone back.
Teach the practical meaning: "When the heart is not pumping well, chest compressions help move blood. Breaths help get oxygen in. Children and infants need both compressions and breaths."
End the slide by reminding students that the course is designed to turn these steps into muscle memory.

tips.title: When will I use CPR
tips.body:
The goal of this slide is to move the training from "theory" to "reality." You want to help your students know exactly what the "Go" signal looks like: Unresponsive and not breathing normally.
• You can achieve this by asking the class: "Think about where you spend most of your time: at the daycare, school, camp, or home. If a child collapsed there right now, who would call 911? Who would get the AED? Where is the closest AED?" This gets them mentally mapping their environment for an emergency.
Acknowledge that statistically, most of them may never need to perform CPR. Frame this as the "Insurance Policy" mindset. We hope we never need it, but we are here so that if that moment ever arrives, we aren't paralyzed by doubt.
Really emphasize the key point by saying: "You start CPR when two things are true. The child or infant is unresponsive, and they are not breathing normally."
• Teach normal breathing in simple terms: "Normal breathing is steady and regular. If the child is gasping, snorting, or breathing irregularly, that does not count. Treat it as an emergency."

tips.title: What if something goes wrong
tips.body:
Address common points of hesitation like:
• "What if I hurt the child?"
• "What if I panic?"
• "What if I do it wrong?"
• "What if I cannot give breaths?"
Acknowledge that this fear is real and it is completely natural to be concerned. Frame the discussion around this simple truth: Doing nothing leaves the child without help. CPR buys time until the AED and EMS arrive.
Regarding giving breaths, remind your class that children and infants need both compressions and breaths. Most pediatric emergencies start as breathing problems, so breaths are critical. This course trains you to give breaths confidently. Practice today so it feels natural when it matters.
IMPORTANT: Do not spend time on rib fracture discussion as a main teaching point. If a student asks, say: "While rib injuries can happen unexpectedly, they are rare in children. If it does occur, continue CPR as normal. If the child is in cardiac arrest, CPR is lifesaving care. Keep going."

tips.title: Good Samaritan Law
tips.body:
Tell your class: "The Good Samaritan Law is a legal principle designed to protect you when you give emergency help to someone who is hurt or in danger. Its main goal is to encourage bystanders like you to give reasonable emergency assistance by providing some legal protections."
As long as a student is acting reasonably, not expecting payment, and trying to help rather than cause harm, they are generally protected.
For childcare providers, add: "If you are working in a childcare or school setting, follow your workplace emergency plan. Call 911 first for life-threatening emergencies. Notify the parent or guardian as soon as it is safe."
Do not promise legal protection. Suggest they check their state attorney general's website for specifics.

tips.title: Course Overview
tips.body:
This slide shows your students the full path of the class. Walk them through the list on the screen, pointing to each item as you speak.
Tell students:
• “Today we will build this one step at a time. First you will learn how to recognize an emergency. Then you will practice child CPR, AED use, infant CPR, and choking care.”
• "You will practice more than once. The goal is not to memorize a speech. The goal is to know what to do with your hands when a real emergency happens."
Instructor Tip: Before each class, make sure your equipment table is ready. You should have an adult or child manikin, an AED trainer, and an infant manikin visible.

tips.title: Recognizing the Emergency
tips.body:
• Everyone’s definition of an emergency is different. If YOU believe it is necessary to call 911, call 911. If it turns out to be a false alarm, that is ok.
• Consider saying: "Know your address before an emergency. In a daycare, school, camp, or home, you should know how to give the exact location.”
Discussion Topics:
• Discuss how a conversation with a 911 dispatcher might go during an emergency. They will likely ask:
• What is your location?
• What is the emergency?
• How many people are hurt?
• Can we have your name and number for a callback? (Remember: You may choose to remain anonymous as a 911 caller)

tips.title: First Actions
tips.body:
Address the adrenaline rush or panic students may feel. It is important to recognize what your body goes through and control your actions in the best way possible.
Teach students to pause and check the scene before approaching the child. You are checking whether it is safe to reach them.
Scene Safety
Tell students: "If the scene is unsafe, do not become another victim. Call 911 and wait for trained responders”
Discussion Topics:
• Examples of scene hazards that might be encountered (i.e. traffic, fire, electric lines, etc)
• What would you do for this individual in the picture? Why or why wouldn't you move them?

tips.title: ASSESSMENT AND ACTIVATION
tips.body:
Before the video, tell students: "Watch for the first actions. Do not worry about perfect wording. Look for the sequence."
Show the video and engage your class to discuss what steps were covered:
1. Recognizing the emergency.
2. Checked for response.
3. Checked for breathing.
4. Called 911.
5. Started compressions

tips.title: Assessment and Activation - Check Responsiveness
tips.body:
Tap the child firmly on both shoulders and shout loudly: "Are you okay?"
Show students what firm taps look like then explain what to watch for.
You can say something like: "A responsive child will give you some sign of life like moving, speaking, crying, blinking, or reacting in any way. If you see any of those, the child does not need CPR, but you may still need to call 911 depending on the situation."
Remind your class that if there is no movement, no sound, and no reaction of any kind, the child is considered unresponsive and they must shout for help, call 911, and get an AED.

tips.title: Assessment and Activation - Getting Help
tips.body:
• Tell your class to avoid generic statements like “Someone call 911!”
• Model it for your students: Point to a specific person and say something like "You in the blue shirt, call 911 and put the phone on speaker." "You by the door, get the AED.”
• The idea is to give the task of finding an AED to someone else so you can remain with the person in need.
Discussion Topics:
• What if you ask a stranger to get you an AED and they don’t know what it is or where to find one?
• What if there is no one else around to help?

tips.title: Assessment and Activation - Check Breathing
tips.body:
• Tell students: "Look at the chest. Is it rising and falling? Is the child breathing normally?" and model it for them.
• Keep it short. Do not let students spend too long trying to decide.
• Teach: "If the child is unresponsive and not breathing normally, start CPR. Gasping, snorting, or irregular breaths are not normal breathing."

tips.title: Assessment and Activation - Begin Chest Compressions
tips.body:
Before moving on, remind the class of the two signs that tell them to act:
1. The child is unresponsive.
2. The child is not breathing.
Tell the class: "When you see those two things together, start CPR right away. Do not check for a pulse. Move directly to compressions.”
• Pulse checks are not part of lay rescuer pediatric CPR because they are not reliable without medical training and can delay compressions.
Use direct language. Do not say "consider beginning CPR."

tips.title: Chest Compression Effect
tips.body:
Definition: The act of pressing down on a child's chest in a rhythmic manner to manually pump blood through the heart and circulate it to vital organs, especially the brain and lungs. If the child's heart is not pumping blood, we are going to pump it from the outside.
Teach: "Chest compressions help move blood when the heart is not pumping well. For a child, push in the center of the chest and keep the rhythm steady.”
Play the video for your class to help visualize what we’re trying to achieve when doing CPR on a victim of cardiac arrest. Since their heart is not beating properly, we must push on their chest and externally pump their heart in order to keep the oxygenated blood flowing and keep the brain alive.

tips.title: Hand Placement
tips.body:
Demonstrate proper hand placement and compressions.
• The heel of your hand should be on the center of the chest, approximately on the lower 1/2 of the sternum.
• Encourage students to keep arms straight and shoulders directly above their hands to reduce fatigue.

tips.title: Compression Depth
tips.body:
Review proper depth and demonstrate.
Teach the rule: "Push about one-third the depth of the chest. For a child that is about 2 inches."
Tell students: "You will not measure this in real life. Practice now so your hands learn what good depth feels like."
While it is important to know proper depth, it can be difficult to measure in a real emergency. Encourage your class to push hard and practice compressions to develop muscle memory.
If a student asks about rib injuries, refer back to the earlier discussion in the "What If Something Goes Wrong" section. Do not let it slow the skill practice.

tips.title: Rate and Rhythm
tips.body:
Teach the number clearly: “Compress at 100 to 120 beats per minute.” Then demonstrate and explain to the students how to read the feedback device on your manikin. For example: “On Prestan manikins you’ll see 2 green lights to let you know you are going the correct rate of 100-120 beats per minute.”
Discussion Topic:
• How fast is 100-120 bpm? Most people don’t know what 100 to 120 beats per minute feels like. A song in that range helps set the pace and build muscle memory during practice. Counting aloud can also help you keep the perfect rhythm.

tips.title: CPR Song
tips.body:
Play the video and demonstrate a full set of 30 compressions while counting out loud. Explain what to look for regarding feedback with the CPR manikins.
Then prepare your class by saying something like: "Now each of you will practice clean, steady compressions prior to adding breaths or an AED."
Make sure you maintain an appropriate student to mannequin ratio.
IMPORTANT: Do NOT call this "hands-only CPR" as the main pediatric skill. In pediatric CPR, students need to learn compressions with breaths.

tips.title: Practice Compressions
tips.body:
• Run the class through multiple rounds of compressions and ensure each student gets a turn to practice.
• Watch for: Proper hand placement, compression depth, rate, and full recoil. Make sure you correct problems right away.
• Encourage students to count compressions aloud.
• If you notice students getting tired, use it as a teaching point: fatigue makes compressions weaker. In a real emergency, switch with another trained rescuer as soon as they are ready.

tips.title: GIVING BREATHS
tips.body:
Administer a barrier device to each student, either a face shield or pocket mask with a 1 way valve, and demonstrate the proper technique:
• Open the airway, pinch the nose, seal the mouth, 1 breath over 1 second, watch for chest rise, deliver second breath.
• Allow each student to practice and assist as needed.
Discussion Topics:
• What happens if I’m not getting chest rise? Ensure you have the airway open, nose plugged, and a good seal around the mouth (or pocket mask)
• How long do I keep trying before getting back to compressions? Keep those pauses in compressions to less than 10 seconds. The longer you stop compressions, the faster blood flow drops off.
• What happens if the child choked on something and I can’t get any air through? If you know they have choked, look in the airway before giving breaths, if you see an item, take it. If you do not, attempt 2 breaths and resume compressions promptly. Do not attempt a blind finger sweep.

tips.title: Practice Giving Breaths
tips.body:
• Run each student through multiple rounds of breaths. Monitor for the skills you demonstrated.
• Ensure chest rise and provide assistance as necessary.
• Have each student practice administering 30 compressions and 2 breaths for 1-2 minutes. You will want these skills to be solid before you add more material with the AED.
Good-to-know: Agonal Breaths
Agonal breaths are abnormal gasping respirations. They are not normal breathing and can happen during cardiac arrest. You may hear gasping, snorting, or irregular breaths. Do not mistake agonal breathing for normal breathing. If the child is unresponsive and only gasping, activate EMS, get an AED, and begin CPR.

tips.title: Using an AED
tips.body:
Prior to starting AED use, do a quick review with the class by saying something like: “As of now, we’ve covered how to recognize the need and do CPR on a child WITHOUT an AED.”
Tell the class: "An AED checks the heart rhythm and tells you whether a shock is needed. Your job is to turn it on, place the pads, follow the prompts, and continue CPR."
How do we use an AED?
• Demonstrate all the components of the AED and how to use it.
• Get out the trainer AED and model putting it on your manikin while listening to the instructions.
• Show and discuss the equipment that might come with an AED with your students such as:
• Gloves, razors, pocket masks, face shields, small towels, wipes, scissors, or shears.
• Remember to mention proper pad placement and that the pads are not interchangeable!
Review these key points with your class:
• The AED should be used as soon as it is available.
• For children younger than 8 years old, use pediatric pads or pediatric settings when available. If they are not available, use adult pads.
• For children age 8 and older, use standard adult pads and settings.
• Make sure the pads do not touch. Use front-and-back placement when needed to keep them separate.
• Follow the AED prompts.
Discussion Topics:
• What if the AED won’t move on to the next step after I’ve attached the pads? Verify that the pads are placed correctly and are making contact with the skin. If you are unable to fix the problem quickly, continue to do chest compressions and breaths. If you have a partner have them troubleshoot working the AED. If it is still not working properly, move the AED to the side and continue doing CPR.
• What if the person is very hairy and the pads won’t stick? Use a razor if available to shave the area where you will be placing the pads. You can also use an extra set of AED pads if they are available and use them to wax the surface.
• What if this is a drowning and they’re all wet? Your AED kit may have a small towel in it. Use this to dry the surface where you will be applying the pads on the chest. You do not need to dry their whole body.
• What if they have an unknown device embedded in their chest where the pad needs to go? If you notice something under the skin, do not place the AED pad directly on top of it, place the pad to the side or just below it. Whether it is a pacemaker or a port, continue the steps to apply the AED and begin CPR. Individuals who have pacemakers can still have AEDs used on them.
• Will I have to fully expose the child to use the AED? No, you only need to expose their chest to apply the AED pads directly to the skin.
• If it’s a girl, do I have to remove or cut the bra? Possibly. If you can retain some modesty and not delay proper care, you would slide the pad under the top strap. However some AEDs may require you to fully expose the woman’s chest in order to apply them properly.

tips.title: Put it all together
tips.body:
• When you get to this slide, leave it up while you run each student through a full scenario. They may use it for reference.
• Multiple people can go at the same time depending on available equipment.
• Make the scenario relevant to their situation.
• Use the skills sheet during this time to evaluate each student’s child CPR/AED skills.
Activity: Practice Scenario
• Explain to the class that they will be running through a full scenario, either alone or with a partner depending on class size and available equipment. Multiple groups may be going at the same time, and multiple AEDs might be operating simultaneously in the same room. It intentionally creates a bit of chaos to help simulate a real emergency where the environment will rarely be calm.
• The scenario will consist of a pretend emergency involving a child who will require CPR. You may create a scenario appropriate to your students or use the example below.
• You may remind them of the things you’re looking for and that you need to hear each person say “Call 911, get an AED” when appropriate. Remember that your goal is for the student to develop confidence in this emergency skill.
Daycare scenario example:
"You are working at a daycare. A 5-year-old is playing outside with the other children. You see the child suddenly collapse onto the ground. The child is not moving. Go."
• Sometimes students start off a bit confused. If so, guide them.
• Some students may forget to call 911 or to check for breathing. If you see this, you can stop them and have them start over.
• If working in groups, you may  need to repeat the scenario to ensure that every student participates in each role and has the opportunity to give compressions, deliver breaths, and put on the AED. Make sure each student knows their rescuer role within their group:
• Rescuer 1 – Compressions
• Rescuer 2 – Breaths/Airway
• Rescuer 3 – AED

tips.title: Infant Assessment
tips.body:
CPR emergencies can be emotionally difficult, particularly when an infant or child is involved.
Tell your class: “An emergency involving an infant can feel especially overwhelming. It is normal to feel nervous or emotional. Take a breath, stay focused, and work through the steps one at a time.”
Inform them that you will be discussing infant mortality and practicing CPR on infant manikins.
Discussion Topic: Causes of infant mortality
• Why would an infant need CPR? Most infant CPR cases start as breathing problems such as choking, drowning, seizures, or suffocation.
• How can caregivers prepare for an infant emergency? By knowing the emergency plan, the location of the phone and AED, and maintaining their training up to date. Regular practice helps everyone respond quickly and calmly.

tips.title: Infant Chest Compressions
tips.body:
Demonstrate proper hand placement techniques for infant chest compressions:
• Heel of one hand: Place the heel of one hand on the sternum in the center of the infant’s chest. Push straight down to compress the chest.
• Two-Thumb encircling hands: Wrap both hands around the infant’s chest and place both thumbs side by side on the sternum in the center of the chest. Push straight down with both thumbs to compress the chest. If unable to encircle the infant’s chest, use the heel-of-one-hand technique.
Activity: Hands‑On Practice
Have students try the heel-of-one-hand and the two-thumb encircling-hands techniques so they can adapt to their own hand size and the situation.
• Run the class through multiple rounds of compressions, ensuring each student gets a turn to practice both techniques.
Do not teach two-finger compressions. This technique was removed from current guidelines

tips.title: Infant Breaths
tips.body:
Tell students: "Infants have small lungs. Give just enough air to see the chest rise. After 30 compressions, give 2 breaths. Each breath lasts about 1 second. Return to compressions quickly."
Demonstrate the correct technique for giving breaths to an infant. Show the class:
• How to position the infant's head in a neutral "sniffing" position: Nose pointing toward the ceiling, not tilted too far back
• How to seal your mouth over the infant's nose and mouth at the same time
• How to give a gentle breath, just enough to see the chest rise, not a forceful or deep breath
• What to do if the chest does not rise: Re-tilt the head, re-check the seal, and try again.
Activity: Hands‑On Practice
Use an infant manikin with a visible chest indicator. Have each student practice head positioning, sealing over the nose and mouth, two gentle breaths, and watching for chest rise.
Watch and correct any mistakes immediately.

tips.title: Infant AED Use
tips.body:
Prior to starting, do a quick review with the class by saying something like:
"We recently covered how to use an AED on a child. Using one on an infant works the same way. The steps do not change. If an AED is available for an infant in cardiac arrest, use it.”
Explain and reinforce these key points:
• Use the AED as soon as it is available
• Use infant or pediatric pads and a pediatric setting when available.
• If pediatric pads or settings are unavailable, use adult pads.
• Make sure the pads do not touch. Place one pad on the chest and one on the back when needed.
• Follow the AED prompts and continue CPR as directed.

tips.title: Infant Scenario
tips.body:
Leave this slide up and run each student through a full infant scenario. Use the skills sheet to evaluate them. You already covered how scenarios work in the child section, so keep the setup brief and get students practicing.
Activity: Infant Practice Scenario
Run a pretend emergency involving an infant who needs CPR. Use the example below or make one that fits your students.
The key difference to watch for: infant emergencies usually start as a breathing problem, so make sure students give real, effective breaths and don't drift into compression-only CPR.
Daycare scenario example:
"You are working in the infant room at a daycare. You go to check on a 6-month-old who has been quiet during nap time. You pick the baby up and notice they are limp and do not respond. Another caregiver is across the room. Go."
• Guide students who start off confused.
• Have them restart if they skip the 911 call, the breathing check, or the breaths.
In groups, repeat the scenario if necessary so each student rotates through every role:
Rescuer 1 – Compressions
Rescuer 2 – Breaths
Rescuer 3 (if available) – AED

tips.title: Mild Choking
tips.body:
Choking is the final major topic and one of the most common real-world emergencies your students will actually face, with both children and infants. Teach recognition before any technique.
Mild choking means the person can still move air.
• Frame it for the class this way: a coughing or crying child or infant is still breathing.
• Make it clear that during mild choking students should not deliver back blows, thrusts, or pats.
• Warn the class that mild choking can escalate to severe quickly, so watching carefully matters.

tips.title: Severe Choking
tips.body:
In severe choking, coughing no longer moves the object and the airway is blocked. A child cannot speak, breathe, or cough and may clutch at the throat. An infant cannot cry, cough, or breathe.
• Stress the urgency. This is the moment to act and send someone to call 911 immediately while relief begins. If alone, begin relief right away and get 911 called as soon as possible.
• Explain that the hands-on technique to clear the airway depends on age, and that a child and an infant are not treated the same. Prepare to demonstrate each technique to your students.
If you cannot see an object that does not belong, DO NOT PERFORM A BLIND FINGER SWEEP

tips.title: Choking Relief Child
tips.body:
• Demonstrate on a child manikin, and get on the child's level first.
• Kneeling or sitting so you are eye to eye keeps the child calmer and puts you at the right angle to deliver effective blows and thrusts.
• Show the cycle: five firm back blows between the shoulder blades, then five abdominal thrusts. Teach back blows first, then thrusts, and have students alternate the two.
Teach the handoff to CPR: If the child becomes unresponsive, gently lower them to the ground, make sure 911 has been called, and begin CPR.
Remind the class that CPR on a choking victim is the same as they already learned, with one added step: before each set of 2 breaths, look in the mouth and remove an object only if you can see it.

tips.title: Choking Relief Infant
tips.body:
If the infant is crying or coughing, air is still moving, so treat it as mild and let them clear it. Move to relief only when the infant can no longer cry, cough, or breathe.
• Demonstrate positioning. Support the infant along your forearm with the chest resting against your arm and a leg on each side of your arm. Keep the head lower than the chest and always support the head and neck.
• Show the cycle: five back blows between the shoulder blades, then flip the infant over and give five chest thrusts using the heel of one hand on the center of the chest. Make it explicit that abdominal thrusts are never used on an infant, because they can injure the organs under the ribs.

tips.title: Practice Infant Choking
tips.body:
• Have your students practice this while sitting down with the infant manikins. Adjust their form as necessary to ensure they are not covering the face.
• The head should stay below the chest. They should perform a series of 5 back blows, and 5 chest thrusts.
Discussion Topics:
• Baby Curiosity: Babies explore with their mouths. So if it fits in their mouth, it goes in their mouth.
• What if the baby goes unresponsive and we haven’t cleared the obstruction? Call 911 and begin CPR.

tips.title: Conclusion
tips.body:
THIS CONCLUDES THE CPR/AED PORTION OF THE COURSE
Thank the class for taking the training seriously and for putting in the effort during hands-on practice and address any questions they may have.
Review the three main takeaways:
• If an infant or child is unresponsive, shout for help, call 911, and send someone to get an AED.
• If they are not breathing normally, begin CPR with chest compressions and breaths.
• When an AED arrives, turn it on immediately, use pediatric pads or settings when available, and follow its prompts.
Close by telling them they should be proud. They now have the knowledge and practice to step in, call for help, begin CPR, and use an AED when it matters.
